content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'highway' functions primarily as a symbol of the prepared way of the Lord—God's route of salvation and deliverance by which He comes to His people and by which the redeemed return to Him. It is most often preached as the 'Highway of Holiness' (Isaiah 35:8): the sanctified path of salvation open to the redeemed and closed to the unclean, and, via Isaiah 40:3, as the way prepared for the coming of Christ, which the Gospels apply to John the Baptist's ministry.","primary_basis":["Isaiah 35:8-10 (the Way/Highway of Holiness for the redeemed returning to Zion)","Isaiah 40:3-5 ('prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God')","Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:2-3; Luke 3:4-6; John 1:23 (Gospel application of Isaiah 40:3 to John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ)","Isaiah 11:16 (a highway for the remnant of God's people, echoing the Exodus)","Isaiah 62:10 ('prepare the way for the people; build up the highway')","John 14:6 (Christ as 'the way,' often linked devotionally to the highway imagery)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Historical-eschatological restoration from exile: the highway as a literal/figurative road for the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon (and Assyria), a second Exodus motif, later extended typologically to salvation in Christ.","basis":["Isaiah 11:16","Isaiah 35:8-10","Isaiah 40:3-4","Isaiah 49:11","Isaiah 57:14","Isaiah 62:10"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The highway as a symbol of the inclusion and reconciliation of the Gentile nations in God's redemptive plan—the eschatological highway linking Egypt, Assyria, and Israel in shared worship.","basis":["Isaiah 19:23-25"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The highway as the sanctified Christian life or journey of holiness—a moral/devotional reading emphasizing progressive sanctification along the 'Way of Holiness' (prominent in Holiness-movement and revivalist preaching).","basis":["Isaiah 35:8","Proverbs 15:19","Proverbs 16:17 ('the highway of the upright is to depart from evil')","Hebrews 12:13-14"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The highway as a call to repentance and removal of moral obstacles—'leveling' and 'straightening' as preparing one's heart for God's coming (a homiletical application of the road-building imagery).","basis":["Isaiah 40:3-4","Isaiah 57:14","Isaiah 62:10","Luke 3:4-6 in context of John's preaching of repentance"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Highways as a negative or neutral image of public exposure, desolation, or judgment—deserted highways signaling societal collapse or divine judgment.","basis":["Judges 5:6 ('the highways were abandoned')","Isaiah 33:8","Lamentations 1:4"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The 'highways and hedges' as a missional symbol of urgent gospel invitation to outsiders and the marginalized.","basis":["Luke 14:23 (Parable of the Great Banquet)","Matthew 22:9-10"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"The consensus is anchored almost entirely in Isaiah, especially 35:8 and 40:3, and in the Gospel writers' explicit citation of Isaiah 40:3 for John the Baptist. Interpreters broadly agree the highway symbolizes God's prepared way of salvation/holiness; differences lie mainly in emphasis (historical return from exile vs. Christological fulfillment vs. personal sanctification vs. Gentile inclusion) rather than in fundamentally competing meanings. These strands are usually treated as complementary layers of a single 'way of the Lord' motif rather than rival interpretations."}
